title: Apple Watch Fall Detection summoning help after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
summary: Fall Detection on an Apple Watch Series 10 called emergency services and alerted emergency contacts when a 69-year-old runner collapsed in cardiac arrest, and he made a full neurological recovery.
headline: An Apple Watch called for help after a runner’s heart stopped
metric: began cardiopulmonary resuscitation about 6–7 minutes after the collapse
brief: A case report published on 12 August 2026 in Resuscitation Plus describes a 69-year-old man who collapsed in ventricular fibrillation while running alone, hidden behind a hedge on a dead-end road.[1] When his Apple Watch detected the fall, it automatically called emergency services on 112 and alerted his emergency contacts. Family members began cardiopulmonary resuscitation about 6–7 minutes after the collapse. An ambulance crew arrived about 1.5 minutes later and defibrillated him, and he made a full neurological recovery. The paper documents that the alerts brought his family to him. It cannot show how long he would have lain there without them, and the comparison rests on an interview in which a son says that he would not otherwise have found his father so quickly.[2] This is a single documented case, echoed by an earlier German report.

title: Empatica Embrace seizure alert reaches Morgan McGrath's mother, who calls paramedics after a seizure left the 26-year-old teacher not breathing (Fulton, Missouri)
summary: An Embrace wristband detected a seizure that left Morgan McGrath, 26, of Fulton, Missouri, not breathing and alerted her mother, who called paramedics; IEEE Spectrum reports that she survived.
headline: *Embrace* wristband alerts a mother, and she calls paramedics
brief: In November 2016 Morgan McGrath, a 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri, had an epileptic seizure that left her unresponsive and not breathing.[1] Her Embrace wristband detected the seizure and alerted her mother, who called paramedics. McGrath survived, and her rescue rests on a single IEEE Spectrum report. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared the device on 26 January 2018, after the event.[2] Later evidence comes from hospital epilepsy monitoring units. In an independent study published on 7 January 2026, researchers in Montreal found that the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures that occurred while it was worn and working, with 29 false alarms in 373 days of monitoring. It detected none of 510 focal seizures without convulsions, a type that the device is not cleared to detect.[3]

title: Lynxight alerts lifeguards to an unconscious swimmer at Inglewood Pool; he recovers fully after rescue
summary: Lynxight, a camera system at a Perth pool, alerted a lifeguard's smartwatch to a man who had sunk unconscious; lifeguards and a swimmer rescued him, and he recovered fully.
headline: Lynxight alerts a Perth lifeguard to a sinking swimmer, who is rescued
brief: On 10 June 2025, a man suffered a medical episode and sank in the outdoor pool at Stirling Leisure - Inglewood in Perth. Lynxight, a camera system built to detect swimmers in distress, sent lifeguard Cameron Menzies a smartwatch alert with the swimmer's location and images. Another swimmer, Ofer Lefelman, noticed the emergency on his own and lifted the man to the surface.[1] Menzies and fellow lifeguards brought him out of the water. title: ASENA analysis program flags a car at Yüksekova carrying 52.5 kg of explosives bound for Istanbul
summary: The Turkish police's ASENA analysis program flagged a car at Yüksekova on 20 March 2022, and officers found 52.5 kg of explosives that the interior minister said were bound for Istanbul.
headline: ASENA flags a car at Yüksekova carrying 52.5 kg of explosives
metric: 133 packets, 52.5 kg, of factory-made explosive
brief: On 20 March 2022 officers of the Hakkari Provincial Police Directorate stopped a car at a checkpoint in Yüksekova, Turkey, after work on the directorate's ASENA analysis program had flagged it. A hidden compartment under the spare-wheel well held 133 packets, 52.5 kg in all, of factory-made explosive assessed as PETN-RDX.[1] The driver was a police officer posted in Istanbul, and on 20 November 2023 the Hakkari 2nd Heavy Penal Court sentenced him to 21 years in prison and four co-defendants to 17.5 years each for supplying weapons to a terrorist organization.[2] ASENA was built to flag drug crime, so this find lay outside its purpose. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said on 21 March 2022 that police using analysis programs, “what they call artificial intelligence”, had identified a suspicious vehicle thought to be carrying drugs.[3] In June 2022 the head of the police Narcotics Crimes Department listed the explosives among the finds of operations that, by his account, had started with ASENA.[4] No source describes the data that ASENA matched for this car or whether an analyst checked the flag before the stop. The driver spoke in court of “those who informed”, but no source reports an informant.[5]

metric: After 4 h 31 min of analysis the system detected him and returned his coordinates
brief: The Bieszczady Mountain Rescue Service called this the first find in Poland of a missing person using a drone and SARUAV.[1] A 65-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease had left home in Cergowa a day after a stroke, and police with tracking dogs did not find him after a storm. On 29 June 2021 the rescue service made four drone flights and ran the SARUAV software on 782 images. After 4 hours and 31 minutes of analysis the software returned his coordinates. Rescuers found him unconscious in grass over two meters tall, after more than 24 hours outdoors, and handed him to the ambulance service. Independent authors wrote that each use of the system needs map data prepared for the area and that SARUAV gives no details on its training data or model architecture.[2] Three of the five authors of the case report work for SARUAV Ltd., and the Polish press quotes the rescue service's own account of the find and describes the failed ground search.[3]

brief: The Department of Justice reported on 30 June 2025 that its analysts and their partners had detected anomalous Medicare billing in Operation Gold Rush. According to the department, the Office of Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services stopped all but about $41 million of about $4.45 billion scheduled for payment.
